title: A blessed Book, sent down to be pondered.
subtitle: Reading to reflect, not just to finish
then: After showing that creation has a purpose, Allah describes the Quran as {reward}a Book full of blessings{/reward}, sent down so that people {idea}ponder its verses{/idea} and those with understanding remember. Ibn Kathir says it teaches sound aims through rational thinking.
now: Ramadan target: finish the whole Quran. You race through pages on your lunch break, barely tasting a word. {idea}One verse understood can do more than ten pages skimmed.{/idea}
old: Reading more pages is what counts.
new: The Book was sent to be pondered, so one verse I reflect on is a real step.
try: Pick one verse today. Read its meaning slowly three times and ask what it says to you.

title: Dawud was given Sulayman: an excellent servant, always turning back.
subtitle: A son praised for repentance, not his crown
then: Allah gave Sulayman to Dawud as a prophet, who {reward}inherited prophethood from him{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says the praise how excellent a servant is because Sulayman was very obedient, worshipped much, and {idea}always turned to Allah in repentance{/idea}.
now: Your parents bragged about your job title at the family dinner. {idea}Allah's praise for a king was about something else: that he kept coming back to Him.{/idea} That is the title worth having.
old: What makes someone excellent is what they achieve.
new: Allah calls a servant excellent for turning back to Him, whatever else they have.
try: Before bed, take one minute to turn back to Allah about something from today.

title: In the afternoon, his finest horses were paraded before him.
subtitle: Good things that fill the eye
then: Sulayman, as king, was shown {reward}well trained horses of the highest breed{/reward} in the afternoon. Mujahid said they stood on three legs and raised the fourth, and were swift. Ibn Kathir also mentions Aishah's toy horse with wings, which made the Prophet ﷺ smile broadly.
now: The new car in the driveway. The renovated kitchen. The laptop you saved for all year. {reward}Nice things are not the enemy.{/reward} But notice how long you stand there looking.
old: Loving good things is either totally fine or totally wrong.
new: Good things are a gift, and also a test of where my attention goes.
try: Thank Allah out loud for one nice thing you own, then put it down and move on.

title: Loving the good made him miss remembering his Lord.
subtitle: Distraction until the sun had set

row.title: own it
sub: I preferred the good over Him

then: More than one scholar said Sulayman was {trap}so busy looking at the horses that he missed Asr{/trap}. It was not deliberate but forgetfulness, like the day of Khandaq when the Prophet ﷺ prayed Asr after sunset. What stands out is that {idea}Sulayman named it plainly{/idea}.
now: You open your phone for one video before Maghrib. You look up and the adhan has long passed. {idea}Say it honestly: I let a good thing pull me away.{/idea} That honesty is the first step back.
old: Missing prayer for something harmless is not a big deal.
new: Even good things can push Allah aside, and I should notice when they do.
try: Set a reminder five minutes before your next prayer and put the phone face down when it rings.

title: Bring them back, he said, and dealt with what distracted him.
subtitle: Two scholarly readings of what he did

row.title: Al-Hasan, Qatadah
sub: he gave them up for Allah

row.title: pure loss
sub: I lose what I let go

then: Scholars differed. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said he gave the horses up, angry for the sake of Allah. Ibn Abbas said {idea}he patted their heads and legs out of love{/idea}, which Ibn Jarir preferred. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah then gave him {reward}the wind, faster and better than horses{/reward}, and cites the hadith: you do not give up anything for Allah but He gives you something better.
now: The game that eats your evenings. The app that keeps you up past midnight. You delete it and feel a small loss. {reward}What Allah gives back is usually better than what you let go.{/reward}
old: If I give something up for Allah, I just lose it.
new: Whatever I leave for Allah's sake, He replaces with something better.
try: Give up one small distraction for today only, for Allah's sake, and see what fills the space.

title: We tested Sulayman, then he turned back.
subtitle: Even a prophet-king was tested
then: Allah says He {trap}tested Sulayman{/trap} and placed a body on his throne. Ibn Kathir does not dwell on details. He says that {reward}after this test, he turned back to Allah{/reward} and asked forgiveness. The heading he gives is how Allah tested Sulayman, then made things easy for him.
now: Everything was going well: the job, the family, the plans. Then something knocks you sideways. {idea}A test is not a sign Allah has left you.{/idea} It is an invitation to come back.
old: If I am being tested, I must have lost Allah's favor.
new: Tests come even to the best of people, and the answer is to turn back to Him.
try: Name one hard thing you are going through and make a short dua about it tonight.

title: Forgive me first, then give me a kingdom like no other.
subtitle: A dua that starts with forgiveness
then: Sulayman asked, {idea}My Lord, forgive me{/idea}, then for a kingdom no one after him would have. The Prophet ﷺ once overpowered a jinn who tried to disturb his prayer and wanted to tie him to a pillar of the masjid, then {reward}remembered the dua of his brother Sulayman{/reward} and let him go.
now: You hold back in dua because your request feels too big: the house, the cure, the job abroad. {reward}Sulayman asked for something unique, and called Allah the Bestower.{/reward} Begin with forgiveness, then ask freely.
old: I should only ask Allah for small, reasonable things.
new: I start by asking forgiveness, then I ask the Bestower boldly.
try: Make one dua today that begins with Astaghfirullah and then asks for something big.

title: The wind was made to run gently at his command.
subtitle: What he let go was replaced with better
then: Al-Hasan Al-Basri said that when Sulayman gave up the horses for the sake of Allah, {reward}Allah compensated him with something better and swifter{/reward}: the wind. Its morning covered a month's journey and its evening a month's journey, blowing gently {idea}wherever in the world he wanted{/idea}.
now: You turned down the overtime that cut into Friday prayer. You worried about the money. Months later, a better door opens. {reward}It rarely looks like a straight swap.{/reward} It is usually better.
old: What I give up for Allah, I expect back in the same form.
new: Allah's replacement can come in a form I never imagined, and better.
try: Recall one thing you once gave up for Allah, and look for what came after it. Say Alhamdulillah.

title: Builders and divers among the jinn worked for him.
subtitle: Power over what others could not reach
then: Ibn Kathir says some jinn {idea}built high rooms, images, basins like reservoirs and fixed cauldrons{/idea}, tasks humans could not do. Others {reward}dived into the sea for pearls and jewels{/reward}. All of it was subjected to Sulayman by Allah.
now: Your team delivers the project. The car starts, the bank transfer goes through, the doctor finds the problem. {idea}So much works for you that you did not make.{/idea} Every helper is a gift placed in your path.
old: What I have achieved is down to my own effort and ability.
new: Everything that serves me was made to serve me by Allah.
try: Thank one person today who makes your work or life easier, and thank Allah for them.

title: And others bound together in chains.
subtitle: Rebellion was restrained, not rewarded
then: Ibn Kathir says those {trap}bound in fetters{/trap} were the ones who had rebelled and refused to work, or whose work was bad and who were wrongdoers. Sulayman's kingdom held power, and {idea}it also held wrongdoing in check{/idea}.
now: You have a temper, a habit, a craving that sometimes runs wild. {idea}Some things in you need to be tied down, not fed.{/idea} Strength includes restraining what does harm.
old: Everything I feel deserves to be let out.
new: Part of strength is restraining what in me does harm.
try: Pick one harmful habit and put one small barrier in its way today.

title: This is Our gift: give or hold back, no account asked.
subtitle: A freedom given, and a choice the Prophet ﷺ made
then: Allah told Sulayman his kingship was {reward}Our gift{/reward}, to give or withhold without being brought to account. Ibn Kathir notes the Prophet ﷺ was given the choice between being a king-prophet or a servant-messenger. He consulted Jibril, who said {idea}be humble{/idea}, so he chose to be a servant.
now: You get to choose: the bigger title with more control, or the quieter role where you serve. {idea}The Prophet ﷺ chose service.{/idea} Both can be good. Humility weighs more with Allah.
old: More control and status is always the better choice.
new: Everything I have is Allah's gift, and humble service is the higher path.
try: Do one quiet act of service today that no one will thank you for.

title: And for him: nearness to Us and a good return.
subtitle: Worldly power did not cost him the Hereafter
then: After all that Allah gave Sulayman in this world, He says Sulayman {reward}will have a great share with Him{/reward} on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir says this refers to {idea}this world and the Hereafter{/idea}. The same words were said of Dawud.
now: You worry that doing well, the raise, the business, the comfortable house, will pull you from Allah. {idea}It does not have to.{/idea} Sulayman had more than anyone and kept turning back.
old: Success in the world and closeness to Allah cannot go together.
new: With gratitude and repentance, what Allah gives me here need not cost me there.
try: Give a little from your next payment to someone in need, as thanks for what you have.
